tagline.text: A small Quezon beach with Boracay sand and Palawan-style cliffs

image.credit: Bitten by a Travel Bug / Public domain / Flickr

children.text: A small beach off Padre Burgos, Quezon, named "Borawan" because it pairs Boracay-like fine sand with Palawan-like limestone cliffs. Island hopping to Dampalitan Island and Puting Buhangin by boat, along with beach camping, are the main draws.

Borawan is a small beach island facing Tayabas Bay off Padre Burgos in southern Quezon, on Luzon. The name blends "Boracay" and "Palawan," capturing how the gray limestone cliffs rising behind the cream-colored sand recall Palawan's El Nido. The beach stretches only a few hundred meters, but with rock, sand, and jade-colored sea all in one frame, it's become known as a photo spot.
It's about
30km
along the west coastal road from the provincial capital Lucena, and about
20–30 minutes

by banca (outrigger boat) from the coastal town of Padre Burgos. Nearby waters hold a scatter of small attractions for island hopping in a single day — Dampalitan Island with its pine-like agoho tree forest, Puting Buhangin in Pagbilao with its fine white sand, and the rock cave Kuweba Lampas.

Borawan Beach is managed by a single locally run resort, divided into several zones with huts, tent spots, and shower and toilet facilities. It is a simple camping beach with no large hotels or restaurant strips, and electricity began arriving in
December 2018
when a submarine cable connecting it to the mainland was laid.

As an island destination only about 5–6 hours from Manila one way, it suits friends packing tents for a weekend camping trip, and budget-conscious travelers who want cliff-and-beach photos. That said, peak-season weekends draw crowds and the beach gets busy, so a weekday visit is best if you want a quiet break.

The huge limestone formations bookending the beach are Borawan's signature feature. Rest in their shade or look for small pockets of sand tucked between the rocks. Photos come out best when morning sunlight hits the cliffs.
Pay a tent-site fee of about
and you can pitch your tent close to the beach. Enjoy the sound of waves and starlight at night, and the sky brightening behind the cliffs in the morning.

blocks.title: The agoho forest on Dampalitan Island

children.text: About 10 minutes by boat from Borawan, Dampalitan Island has pine-like agoho trees lining its beach, creating an exotic scene. A stop here at sunset is a popular route.

Puting Buhangin, near Pagbilao, is true to its name — a beach of fine "white sand" — while nearby Kuweba Lampas is a cave that cuts straight through the rock. An island-hopping trip linking all three islands lets you see them together.
At high tide, the water off the beach is calm and good for swimming. You can spot small fish on the shallow bottom around the rocks, though it's not a place to expect vivid coral reefs.
In peak season, you can rent kayaks and banana boats and other water sports gear on the beach. Availability and prices vary day to day, so check on-site.

Grilling fish and meat bought at the mainland market right on the beach is one of the joys of camping at Borawan. With so little light on the island, clear nights bring stars pouring down over the silhouette of the cliffs.

When chartering a banca, it's common to arrange both the first day's island hopping and the second day's return trip in a single booking. A day trip is possible too, but with so much travel time, you'll have less time on the beach itself.
Lucena-bound buses (JAC Liner, JAM Liner, DLTB, Lucena Lines, and others) leave frequently from Cubao and Buendia in Manila. To the Lucena Grand Terminal it takes about
3–4 hours
and the fare is about
From Lucena Grand Terminal, take a minibus or jeepney bound for Unisan or Agdangan and get off in Padre Burgos town proper. It takes about
45 minutes–1 hour 15 minutes
, for a fare of about
. Ask the driver to let you off near the pier for Borawan.
From Padre Burgos town proper, a tricycle or motorbike taxi to a banca pier such as Aplaya or Vasiao takes about
10–15 minutes
, for a fare of about
There's no scheduled ferry — you charter a banca. A round trip to Borawan alone costs about
per boat, or about
per boat if you add Dampalitan and Puting Buhangin, usually seating up to 8–10 people. It takes about
20–30 minutes
from the pier to Borawan.
Fares vary by pier and season, and often don't include entrance fees. Before you set off, be clear on what's included and agree on a pickup time for your return day.
Take SLEX, continue on Maharlika Highway from Santo Tomas, and pass the outskirts of Lucena to reach Padre Burgos — about
4–5 hours
. Leave your car with a household or a private lot near the pier for about
Southern Quezon's coast has a short, indistinct dry season with fairly even rain year-round, but
February–May
sees the least rain and the calmest seas, making it the best time for island hopping and camping. In
April–May
, midday temperatures climb to
and summer break overlaps with Holy Week, making the beach most crowded. If you want fewer people and clearer water, a weekday just outside peak season is best.
June–October
brings the southwest monsoon and typhoon season, with high waves on many days, and
November–January

also sees frequent rain from the northeast monsoon. Bancas don't run when a small-craft warning is issued, so check PAGASA forecasts and coast guard notices, and keep your schedule flexible in the wet season. The water can turn cloudy on overcast days or right after rain.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
To stay on Borawan, use the tent spots or huts at the beach resort. Tent spots cost about
and huts about
, and showers and toilets sometimes carry a separate fee. Electricity is available, but many people charge their phones at the resort's paid charging station (about
per charge). If tents are uncomfortable, you can also stay at a small resort on the Padre Burgos mainland coast or a hotel in Lucena (about
per night) and make day trips to the island.

Shops and eateries on the island have limited menus and higher prices, so many travelers buy meat, fish, rice, water, and ice in Lucena market or Padre Burgos town and grill it themselves on the beach. Some sections restrict bringing in outside food, so check when you arrive. On the way back, it's worth trying Quezon specialties in Lucena — pancit habhab (noodles) and sweet Lucban longganisa.
There's no ATM on the island. Bring enough cash, especially small bills, to cover the banca, entrance fees, and tent fee.
The more people in your banca, the lower the per-person cost. If you're traveling alone, sharing a boat with other travelers at the pier is another option.
Buy drinking water and ice on the mainland. Prices on the island run nearly double.
Phone charging is limited, so bring a power bank and a flashlight.
It's best to take photos around
6–8 AM
, when there are fewer people. By day the beach fills with tents and visitors.
Tent sites can be scarce on peak-season weekends and Holy Week, so a weekday visit or calling ahead is recommended.
The width of the beach and the best swimming times shift with the tide. Check the tide table and plan swimming around high tide, and rock-side walks around low tide.
Bring trash bags and carry all your garbage back out. The island lacks proper waste facilities.
On the
official website
of Borawan Island Resort, which runs Borawan Beach, you can check room and tent reservations, island hopping, and kayak rates (about
per hour). Book ahead for peak-season weekends.
There have been reports of jellyfish in these waters. Wear a rash guard, and if stung, rinse with vinegar and head straight to a mainland hospital if symptoms are severe.
The limestone rocks are sharp and slippery when wet. Wear sneakers when climbing on them and don't push your limits.
If a small-craft or typhoon warning is issued, bancas won't run and you could be stranded on the island.
Wear a life vest when riding a banca, and avoid boats carrying more passengers than their capacity.
Entrance fees and banca rates change often depending on the operator, so confirm current rates on-site.
On crowded days, theft of belongings can happen, so keep valuables on your person.
